passage: Raghav flicked rules away like dust. "Babies," he said to Chinmay, who had refused to bunk the last period and ride bikes on the highway without helmets. Omkar's stomach clenched. He had gone along the week before, laughing at the wrong moment because he feared being left out. This time he said quietly to Chinmay at the bike stand, "Can I say no with you?" Chinmay grinned. "Sure. Just say, not today, I've got homework. Keep it short." When Raghav sneered, Omkar used exactly those words, and Chinmay added, "Come for chai after school, though." Nobody lectured Raghav, and he shrugged. The next day Ma'am asked where Raghav had been. Omkar started to say, "He was sick," then stopped: Raghav had told them he had tried a stunt on a wall and hurt his wrist. Omkar told Raghav, "I'm not going to lie for you, but I care what happens to you. Show your wrist to the nurse." Raghav went. That afternoon Omkar told the class teacher what he knew, without mocking anyone.

qa.q: What did Chinmay refuse to do?
qa.a: Chinmay refused to bunk the last period and ride bikes on the highway without helmets.

qa.q: How did Omkar's earlier going along differ from his later refusal, and what did Chinmay's example add?
qa.a: Earlier Omkar laughed along because he feared being left out; later he refused with an ally and a short reply, and Chinmay stayed friendly without lecturing, which made saying no easier.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when Raghav called Chinmay a baby?
qa.a: His stomach clenched, so he felt afraid of being laughed at or left out.

qa.q: What did Omkar do about Raghav's hurt wrist, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He refused to lie for Raghav, urged him to see the nurse and told the class teacher, showing loyalty to Raghav's wellbeing rather than to the risky stunt.

grounding: Four teenagers meet peer pressure to bunk and take risks: contempt for rule-followers, going along from fear, covering for a friend and a friend who refuses and is followed.
